title: Duchenne and Becker Muscular Dystrophy
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: X‑linked dystrophinopathies cause progressive muscle weakness due to loss of membrane stability. Duchenne presents early with severe weakness; Becker is milder and later onset. Management is supportive and focuses on cardiac and respiratory complications.

sections.p: Duchenne (DMD) and Becker (BMD) muscular dystrophy are caused by mutations in the DMD gene that abolish or reduce dystrophin, a protein that links the cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma. Loss of dystrophin makes muscle fibers fragile, leading to necrosis, replacement by fat/fibrosis and progressive weakness.
b: X‑linked recessive; affects boys, female carriers usually asymptomatic
DMD: frameshift or nonsense mutation → no functional dystrophin
BMD: in‑frame deletions → truncated but partially functional dystrophin

sections.p: Dystrophin forms a complex with dystroglycans, sarcoglycans and syntrophins, stabilising the sarcolemma during contraction. It also anchors nitric oxide synthase, influencing muscle perfusion.
b: Normal dystrophin: ~427 kDa protein spanning the membrane
Protects against stretch‑induced calcium influx
Maintains sarcolemmal integrity and signaling

sections.p: The DMD gene is one of the largest human genes (2.2 Mb, 79 exons). Transcription is tightly regulated during myogenesis; alternative promoters produce tissue‑specific isoforms (e.g., Dp71 in brain).
b: X‑inactivation in females can produce mild symptoms in carriers
Up‑regulation of utrophin (a dystrophin homologue) is a therapeutic target

sections.p: Mutations truncate or eliminate dystrophin, causing sarcolemmal tears with each contraction. Calcium overload triggers proteases, leading to fibre necrosis, inflammation and replacement by fibrofatty tissue.
b: DMD: onset 2‑3 y, loss of ambulation ~10‑12 y, cardiomyopathy by early teens
BMD: onset adolescence or early adulthood, slower loss of ambulation, later cardiac disease
Elevated CK >10 000 U/L in early disease, then declines as muscle mass wanes

sections.p: Patients present with delayed motor milestones, Gowers’ sign, calf pseudohypertrophy and progressive weakness. Cardiac involvement (dilated cardiomyopathy) and respiratory failure are the main causes of mortality.
b: Gowers’ sign: using hands to rise from floor indicates proximal weakness
Calf pseudohypertrophy: fat infiltration mimics hypertrophy
Serial echocardiography and pulmonary function tests are essential

t.b: Is there muscle breakdown? – Very high (>10 000 U/L) supports dystrophinopathy; normalizes later
What mutation is present? – Detects deletions/duplications or point mutations; confirms diagnosis and informs carrier testing
What is the pattern of involvement? – Shows fatty infiltration; useful when genetic testing unavailable
Is cardiac function impaired? – Detects early systolic dysfunction; guides ACE‑inhibitor therapy
Is respiratory reserve falling? – Decline in FVC predicts need for non‑invasive ventilation

sections.p: No cure; treatment aims to preserve muscle, cardiac and respiratory function and to prevent complications.
b: Corticosteroids (prednisone or deflazacort) – slow loss of ambulation, improve pulmonary function; monitor for growth suppression and hypertension
ACE inhibitors or ARBs – start when ejection fraction <55 %; reduce progression of cardiomyopathy
Non‑invasive ventilation (BiPAP) – when FVC <1 L or nocturnal hypoventilation; improves survival
Physiotherapy with stretching and low‑impact aerobic exercise – maintains range of motion, prevents contractures
Orthopaedic interventions (spinal fusion for scoliosis) – indicated for progressive curve >40°

t.b: Rely on CK, family history and clinical picture; refer for muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for dystrophin
Use clinical signs (tachycardia, hepatomegaly) and ECG (deep Q waves, LVH) to trigger empirical ACE‑inhibitor therapy

sections.p: Other progressive neuromuscular disorders that cause proximal weakness.
b: Spinal muscular atrophy – lower motor neuron disease, no calf hypertrophy, normal CK
Limb‑girdle muscular dystrophy – autosomal recessive, later onset, CK moderately raised
Polymyositis – inflammatory, responds to immunosuppression, elevated ESR/CRP

sections.p: CK can be falsely low in advanced disease when muscle mass is depleted; normal CK does not exclude a milder Becker phenotype.
b: Mild Becker may have CK 2‑5 × upper limit only
Acute exercise can transiently raise CK, mimicking dystrophy

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid decline in respiratory function (dyspnoea at rest, O₂ saturation <90%)
New onset chest pain or palpitations suggesting arrhythmia
Sudden loss of ambulation or severe contractures

faq.q: Why do DMD patients develop calf pseudohypertrophy?
faq.a: Fat and connective tissue replace degenerated gastrocnemius fibres, giving a bulky appearance.
Rarely; skewed X‑inactivation can produce mild muscle weakness or cardiomyopathy.

faq.q: Is a muscle biopsy still needed?
faq.a: Only when genetic testing is unavailable; immunostaining shows absent or reduced dystrophin.

exam: What bedside signs differentiate Duchenne from Becker muscular dystrophy? — Gowers’ sign and age of loss of ambulation; Becker retains ambulation longer.

A 4‑year‑old boy presents with delayed walking and calf hypertrophy. CK is 12 000 U/L. Which test confirms the diagnosis and why? — Genetic testing (MLPA/NGS) to identify DMD gene mutation; it guides prognosis and carrier testing.
How does loss of dystrophin lead to muscle fibre necrosis? — Membrane fragility allows calcium influx, activating proteases that destroy sarcomeres.
When should ACE‑inhibitor therapy be started in a Duchenne patient? — When echocardiography shows ejection fraction <55 % or early ECG changes, even before symptoms.

Explain why corticosteroids improve ambulation but have significant side‑effects. — They reduce inflammation and membrane leakage, slowing fibre loss; chronic use causes growth suppression, weight gain, and osteoporosis.
A patient cannot undergo MRI due to lack of equipment. How would you still assess disease extent? — Use clinical muscle strength grading, CK trends, and, if possible, ultrasound of thigh muscles.
What are the indications for non‑invasive ventilation in Duchenne? — FVC <1 L, nocturnal hypoventilation, or daytime hypercapnia; improves quality of life and survival.
Why is utrophin up‑regulation a therapeutic target? — Utrophin can substitute for dystrophin at the sarcolemma, potentially stabilising the membrane.
